title: Standardized patient: breathlessness
intro: Door card: Mrs. Margaret Holloway, 71, "short of breath". Fifteen minutes for a history and a focused cardiovascular and respiratory exam.

steps.say: Mrs. Holloway sits propped up on the exam table, a little breathless as she says hello, her ankles puffy over the tops of her shoes.

options.text: Introduce yourself, then ask if she's comfortable sitting up like that before you start.
options.reply: "Sitting up's the only way I can breathe, dear. Thank you for asking."

options.text: Ask her to lie flat so you can start the exam straight away.
options.reply: She tries, then sits up again, gasping. You've learned something, the hard way.

options.text: Start with the history without introducing yourself.
options.reply: She answers, but she keeps glancing at your badge.

choice.lesson: Introduce yourself and make the patient comfortable before anything else

history.opening: "I just can't get my breath like I used to. It's been getting worse for weeks."

items.ask: When did this start, and how far can you walk now?
items.answer: "Three weeks or so. Now I'm puffed walking to the mailbox."

items.ask: Is it worse lying flat? How many pillows do you sleep on?
items.answer: "Three pillows. If I lie flat I feel like I'm drowning."

items.ask: Do you ever wake up at night short of breath?
items.answer: "Twice this week I woke up gasping and had to sit on the edge of the bed by the window."
"My ankles are like balloons by evening. My shoes don't fit."
"Up four kilos this month, and I'm not eating more."
"A dry cough at night. No fever."

items.ask: Have you had heart problems before?
items.answer: "A heart attack six years ago. They put a stent in."

items.ask: Do you have high blood pressure or diabetes?

items.answer: "Aspirin, a cholesterol pill, and a water pill I stopped last month. I was running to the bathroom all day."

items.ask: Has anything changed in what you eat?
items.answer: "My grandson's been bringing takeout most nights. It's so salty."

maneuvers.name: Vital signs
maneuvers.finding: BP 148/88, HR 96 and irregularly irregular, RR 22, SpO₂ 92% on room air, no fever.

maneuvers.name: Look at the neck veins
maneuvers.finding: At 45°, the jugular venous pressure is raised: 8 cm above the sternal angle.

maneuvers.name: Listen to the heart
maneuvers.finding: Irregularly irregular, with a third heart sound and a soft pansystolic murmur at the apex.

maneuvers.name: Listen to the lungs
maneuvers.finding: Fine crackles at both bases, a third of the way up.

maneuvers.name: Press on the ankles and shins
maneuvers.finding: Pitting edema to mid-shin on both legs.

maneuvers.name: Feel the abdomen
maneuvers.finding: The liver edge is 2 cm below the ribs and a little tender.

steps.question: sp_dysp_orthopnea_01
steps.lead: In the debrief, your preceptor asks:

choice.prompt: Before you leave, Mrs. Holloway says quietly, "I stopped the water pill because I couldn't leave the house. I suppose that was silly."

options.text: "It's not silly: a lot of people struggle with that. Could we ask your doctor about taking it at a time that fits your day, like after your morning errands?"
options.reply: She brightens. "I could take it when I get back from church."

options.text: "You really shouldn't have stopped it. That's why you're unwell."
options.reply: She looks at her hands. "I know."

options.text: "Just take it every day, whatever happens."
options.reply: She nods, but you can tell she won't.

choice.lesson: Explore why a medicine was stopped and solve the problem together, without blame

feedback: "Thorough and kind. You found the missed diuretic and the salt, which is where the fix is."
"Good. In breathlessness, always ask about orthopnea, PND, edema and weight."
"Review the signs of heart failure: JVP, crackles, S3, edema. Then practice this one again."
